title: 3-Read Friday #17: Teaching Klaxons, Checking for Listening, and the First 10 Minutes
author: Craig Barton
summary: Craig Barton's 3-Read Friday #17 curates three posts on everyday classroom habits, good and bad. Tom Sherrington lists ten common "klaxon" moments -- things teachers say or do that quietly undermine their own goals, from dead-end checks for understanding to leaving a struggling student hanging in front of the class. Adam Robbins compares two near-identical ways of using the same explanation slide, showing how simply reordering when a question is asked can shift the "think ratio" and change whether students are really listening. Jody Chan walks through her deliberately scripted first ten minutes of a lesson -- entry routine, silent starter, and circulating with a "magical marking pen" -- and the reasoning behind each step. Barton frames the set as proof that small, repeatable routines, not big new initiatives, are where most classroom improvement actually happens.
points: Tom Sherrington's ten "klaxons" -- including dead-end checks for understanding and hanging a struggling student out to dry in front of the class -- name specific, avoidable habits rather than vague advice.
Adam Robbins shows that asking a checking-for-listening question before revealing an answer on a slide, rather than after, raises the "think ratio" even though the visible content is identical.

Jody Chan's scripted first-ten-minutes routine -- fixed entry procedure, silent retrieval starter, visible timer, and circulating to check work -- is designed to be habitual enough that students feel safe knowing what to expect.
Barton's selections this week are unified by a practice-and-culture register: classroom habits, routines, and small talk-moves rather than curriculum content or research findings.
